#3458. The Rookie's Expansion Series Officially Caps Off 2026 With The Best News

The news that The Rookie: North has already wrapped its first season of filming proves that The Rookie franchise’s next outing is in good stead heading into 2027. It is tough for any cop show to stand out in 2026, and even tougher for a cop show to pull off this achievement on network TV. Between the NCIS, Law & Order, FBI, and 9-1-1 franchises, there is no shortage of procedural shows on network TV, and a mere gimmick isn’t necessarily enough to make a cop show stand out anymore.

Admittedly, Person of Interest’s vision of future policing made the Jonathan Nolan series a critical hit, but that show began over a decade ago. More recently, 2018’s Nathan Fillion vehicle The Rookie managed to subtly sell a classic cop procedural by starting out with an unusual premise. Loosely based on a real-life officer’s experience, Fillion’s 40-year-old John Nolan became the LAPD’s youngest “rookie” ever as the series began.

As Nolan became more at home in policing and his comparatively advanced age was no longer such a major plot point, The Rookie subtly transitioned into being more of a traditional ensemble cop show than a character study. While the clunky Yellowstone spinoff Marshals practically audibly switches gears when the series shifts from focusing on its main character to the rest of the team, The Rookie’s inseparable crew became so popular that the show eventually spawned the upcoming spinoff The Rookie: North.

The Rookie: North will not technically mark the first spinoff of the series, thanks to 2022’s The Rookie: Feds. However, that earlier series lasted only one season, while The Rookie: North already has a more promising future ahead of it. Set in Washington State, The Rookie: North sees Top Gun: Maverick’s Jay Ellis star as Alex Holland, the newest recruit of the Pierce County Police Department.

In a TikTok video, Ellis announced that The Rookie: North season 1’s production officially wrapped filming in late November 2026, meaning show runner Alexi Hawley’s show is already in the can prior to its premiere. This is a surprisingly pivotal benefit to the show, as evidenced by another, more famous Washington State-set police procedural. When episodes are produced week upon week, characters, plots, and planned story arcs can be revised depending on audience reactions.

This might sound like a winning system, but the fate of David Lynch and Mark Frost’s iconic murder mystery Twin Peaks proves it is not that simple. Essentially, when the show’s writers don’t necessarily have a version of the story for the show and all of its episodes already locked in before its debut, pressure from executives can result in massive changes that don’t necessarily make sense in the long run.

Since Frost and Lynch were busy with other projects during the production of Twin Peaks season 2, the show rapidly declined in quality as the writers scrambled to pad out its increasingly bloated and bizarre story. Luckily, The Rookie: North has already avoided this issue in season 1 since, with filming wrapped before the premiere, the show can’t be expected to take on feedback until season 2 at the earliest.

The Rookie: North’s synopsis teases Ellis’s protagonist joining the police, despite his older age, after a terrifying home invasion makes him reconsider his life path. The show’s supporting cast includes The Boys star Karen Fukuhara, Scarpetta’s Janet Montgomery, and Murder in a Small Town’s Mya Lowe, as well as Cruel Summer supporting star Froy Gutierrez.

Due to debut on ABC in January 2027, The Rookie: North will arrive exactly one year after The Rookie’s season 8 debut. With an impressive streaming audience and live ratings alike, The Rookie shows no sign of ending any time soon despite The Rookie: North expanding its franchise.

#3457. Reese Witherspoon’s Forgotten 8-Part Miniseries Is a Near-Perfect Binge

Reese Witherspoon can do it all, from breezing through law school in pink heels in Legally Blonde to alpha-momming her way down student halls in Big Little Lies. We can always depend on her for a gripping performance, and one of her most compelling roles is worth revisiting.

In Hulu's Little Fires Everywhere, Witherspoon once again steps into a Big Little Lies-esque maternal position in a wealthy community, but this time, she goes toe to toe with Kerry Washington. Both actors are magnetic on the screen together, creating a back-and-forth relationship that forces us to look at motherhood in a fresh light. All eight episodes are on Hulu, and watching these two get under each other's skin makes for a satisfyingly tense weekend binge.

Adapted from the novel of the same name by Celeste Ng, Little Fires Everywhere wastes no time throwing us into its central mystery of Elena's (Witherspoon) family house being set on fire. Cue the time jump to four months prior. Elena is exactly the kind of mother you would expect to find in the late-1990s, wealthy American suburb, Shaker Heights, one who meticulously curates her image and enriches her four high school kids' college applications with suitable extracurriculars. She also decides to rent out her family's rental property — at a charitable price — to a single mother and nomadic artist, Mia Warren (Washington), and her teenage daughter, Pearl (Lexi Underwood).

A one-hit wonder is not a failure, it is a band that got one thing exactly right and never had to do it twice. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best song on the list.

You are the one who starts it. This is a song that speeds up, slows down, changes key and ends somewhere nobody predicted, and it still gets an entire room on its feet in under four seconds, which is a decent description of how you operate.

You do not stay down. The entire song is one idea repeated until you believe it, which is exactly how resilience works in practice, and it is why it has soundtracked roughly every sporting comeback filmed since 1997.

You feel it all and you want it on the record. This is a breakup song that stops halfway through to let the other person answer back, which almost no breakup song does, and it is why it sounds less like a complaint and more like a transcript.

Nobody can quite account for you, and you are fine with that. This is a fuzzed-out gospel rock song written by a Jewish folk singer who had been watching country gospel on television, and the fact that it works at all is the whole point.

As the families become more intertwined through friendship and Elena's even more charitable offer of a job as a "house manager" to Mia, the tension between the two mothers steadily increases. Mia harbors a mysterious past and, as an investigative journalist, Elena can't quite let it go. When a custody battle over a baby girl also comes into play, the two mothers take opposite stances, which incites another exploration into their past traumas. Throughout the eight episodes, the conflict between them is riveting, especially as the show steadily unpacks motherhood with the nuances of class and racial differences.

As the title suggests, there are Little Fires Everywhere in this series, where each storyline ignites its own set of themes and tension, but the driving force of the show is motherhood. Much of it boils down to the complicated relationship between Elena and Mia, who are both drawn to and repulsed by each other's lifestyles, parenting behaviors, secrets, and identities. In the very first episode, there's an instance where Pearl and Elena's son, Moody (Gavin Lewis), aredriven home by neighborhood security due to trespassing. Elena scolds Moody, but very easily brushes the incident off, while Mia is rattled and reminds Pearl that the cops react differently to them. The show is quick to establish the differences between the mothers' circumstances, exacerbated by the later custody battle.

While Elena and Mia's approaches to parenting and their identities remain at the center, the custody battle further unravels layers of the show's discourse around the nuances of motherhood. It is a grueling case between Bebe Chow, who left her infant daughter at a fire station when she could no longer afford to feed her, and Linda McCullough, who has been raising the baby and hopes to adopt her. There is never a moment when we firmly believe one side should win, even as Elena and Mia make their stances obvious and crusade against each other. Little Fires Everywhere thrives in the gray area, never shying away from the bitter reality.

Though the rhetoric is heavy and harrowing, the way the show weaves its storytelling together allows us to be fully immersed. It ties the custody battle thoughtfully into Elena and Mia's rivalry and backstories, building on each other to paint this intricate portrait of motherhood. By also maintaining the rich and dynamic characterizations of these two opponents, the show anchors its wider commentary into our personal investment in their development. It's truly a captivating way to approach a timeless concept, one that you can easily lose yourself in during a weekend binge.

With motherhood at the crux of the show, it is only natural that Witherspoon and Washington take the brunt of the responsibility of conveying its nuance. Similar to her role in Big Little Lies, Witherspoon hits the mark of the "perfect" suburban mother, but there's also an underlying desperation in Elena as she fights to control her black sheep daughter or walks on eggshells around Mia in fear of accidentally saying something offensive. Opposite her is Washington's erratic, suspicious, jaded, and equally desperate Mia, who balances parenting with her career and her trauma, never knowing where to draw the line. But together, they are arresting.

Witherspoon and Washington take to their roles beautifully, sustaining a chemistry and tension that is palpable whenever they are on-screen. Their micro-expressions clearly convey the attraction and discomfort Mia and Elena have at the beginning of the series, skirting the line artfully so we are hanging on their every twitch. As the relationship evolves into a more fearsome rivalry, their emotions feel primordial and vicious while maintaining an empathetic vulnerability that fleshes out the contentious nature of motherhood. We watch them make mistakes and struggle with impossible decisions, while still trying to cling to pieces of their identity outside of being a mother. It's a dizzying combination that sucks you right in.

“What, like it's hard” to love Witherspoon in everything she does?

These two are the powerful duo we never knew we needed to see on the screen together, so Little Fires Everywhere needs to be on your watchlist. As they bring their characters to life with moving performances, they flesh out the show's driving exploration of motherhood, one that never backs out from facing tiny details often left forgotten. With taut tension and emotion maintained throughout its eight episodes, the show makes for a gripping and gratifying experience, topped with two wildly overlooked performances.

As anyone who has ever shopped at The Home Depot (or any hardware store) knows, power tools are expensive. That’s why Black Friday at The Home Depot is so important: It’s the perfect opportunity to get the tools you’ve been wanting at some pretty steep discounts. And the best deals even give you a free tool if you purchase a starter kit from one of the major tool brands (Ryobi, DeWalt, Makita, or Milwaukee).

Here’s how this year's “buy one, get one” (BOGO) deal works: Pick out a starter kit from one of the brands, add it to your cart, and you’ll be presented with a list of available tools you can add (they’ll be marked “FREE,” so you can’t get confused). When you go to check out, the price of the tool will be listed as “SAVINGS.”

Here are the starter kits you can choose from:

Ryobi ONE+ 18V Starter Kit (includes one 4.0Ah and one 2.0Ah battery and charger). Cost: $99.

DeWalt 20V Max Starter Kit (includes 6.0Ah and 4.0Ah batteries and charger). Cost: $199.

Makita 18V LXT Starter Pack (includes two 5.0Ah batteries and a rapid charger). Cost: $199.

Milwaukee M18 FUEL Combo Kit (includes a brushless, cordless hammer drill and an impact driver). Cost: $399.

Note that the Ryobi, DeWalt, and Milwaukee offers include 14 free tools to choose from, while the Makita offer only includes 8. Also, note that while the Ryobi starter kit is your cheapest option for a free tool, the batteries included are weaker. The DeWalt or Makita batteries cost more, but offer more power and flexibility.

Some of the deals go beyond just getting a freebie. For example, if you choose the DeWalt Starter Kit for $199, you can get an Atomic 20V Max impact wrench that normally costs $239 for free, which is a significant savings even if you already have batteries and a charger and don’t really need those items (plus, you can never have too many batteries).

The Home Depot is also offering deep discounts on just about everything in the store. Some of the most notable tool deals include:

50% off this DeWalt Cordless Brushless Oscillating Multi Tool, including battery and charger

33% off this Ryobi Combo Kit, an incredible deal for a circular saw, reciprocating saw, and a power drill/driver plus two batteries and a charger; the batteries are small, but this is a great deal on a starter kit.

42% off this Combo Kit from Milwaukee, including a Packout toolbox, a hammer drill, an impact driver, a grinder, and a reciprocating saw, plus two batteries and a charger—a massive deal for anyone who needs to tool up rapidly.

45% off this Brushless Cordless Impact Wrench Kit from Ryobi, which includes a battery and charger.

That only scratches the surface—if you’ve ever needed anything from Home Depot, Black Friday is the day to run out and get it.

Of course, Black Friday can be a little chaotic, so here are a few tips to maximize your savings and experience:

Check online and in-store. Some deals are in-store only, and some items (especially BOGO tools) may not be available at your nearest location—make sure you enter your ZIP code when you’re checking out to ensure you won’t have any problems.

Consider whether you need more batteries and chargers. Depending on your existing collection of batteries and chargers, buying more to get the discount may or may not make sense.

There's no price matching or rain checks. Remember that the store won’t honor price-matching or offer rain checks on Black Friday items.

Cyber Monday will have deals, too. More deals will be rolled out on Cyber Monday (November 30), which may include items you want but don’t see on sale for Black Friday. But keep in mind that Black Friday prices probably won’t go any lower—so snap up what you need as soon as you can.

Sign up for text alerts to save a little more. Home Depot offers a $5 coupon (off a purchase of $50 or more) when you sign up for email or text alerts, which you may be able to apply to your Black Friday purchase for a little extra savings.

Home Depot isn’t the only store offering free tool giveaways:

Like Home Depot, Lowes is offering BOGO tools with the purchase of starter kits from major tool brands.

Tractor Supply Co. has a wide range of BOGO tool offers during its Black Friday Event.

If you’re looking for outdoor equipment, note that Bass Pro Shops and Cabela’s aren’t offering a BOGO deal this year, but the first 250 customers at each physical store will receive a free “mystery promo card” valued between $10 and $500. If you’re going to go for this, plan to line up early—250 cards are going to go fast.

The best early deals on tools right now are at Home Depot, where you can get up to 65% off on select Milwaukee tools, 50% off on DeWalt tools, and 30% off on Ryobi tools. They also have several offers for over 50% off on hand tools..

Home Depot and Lowe’s often compete with each other for seasonal sales, so it’s always a good idea to check both sites before buying. Right now, Home Depot has the best deals on DeWalt and Milwaukee cordless tool sets, but Lowe’s has a better deal on Craftsman hand tool sets.

The best prices of the year on tools are during the holidays in November and December. This is because of the holiday shopping push, as well as making space for new tools that come out in the spring. The second-best time to buy tools is in May and June during Father’s Day sales.

#3455. Apple Watch SE 3 vs Series 12: Which should you buy this holiday season?

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift. Apple’s lineup includes the affordable Apple Watch SE 3 and the more advanced Apple Watch Series 12.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up…

The Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a big update last year, adding a variety of new higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

The Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

Even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a big update over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-new Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the company conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”

With the new system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

As I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The new sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

The Apple Watch lineup is incredibly strong right now. Whether you’re deciding between the SE 3 and Series 12, both offer great health tracking, battery life, and connectivity. The Apple Watch SE 3 is an excellent choice for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem.

The Apple Watch Series 12, however, is the best Apple Watch for most people. There are major improvements to the health tracking capabilities, offering meaningful steps forward in what the Apple Watch can tell you about yourself. In the two months I’ve had mine, I’ve come to appreciate the more frequent heart rate measurement and readiness score.

#3454. How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

Every visual element in animation helps tell the story. That’s especially useful when you’re trying to do something new inside the long, proud tradition of Disney animated movies where magic is afoot. “Hexed” is exactly that: the story of a young girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who learns there’s more to life than her small-town Ohio hometown and more to her family, particularly her mother Alice (Rashida Jones), than meets the eye.

And by “more,” we mean witches. Lots of witches.

“Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others. In a way, much of it feels familiar to recent Disney Animation Studios fare: A secret world of wonder and magic awaits just around the riverbend and/or through a magic portal, accessible only by imbuing one’s inner spark with “witchification.” But there is still something fundamentally broken about that magic world that our protagonist is positioned to make happen. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

And by “something,” “Hexed” Celeste (Jodie Foster), the queen of the hidden realm of Hexe, who is waiting to complete a moonlit ritual that will change the world forever.

According to Miller, the “Hexed” team differentiates this world from the magic of others in the Disney Vault through character design. “ If you look at Billie, you look at Alice, and you look at Celeste, I think we see their personalities come forward,” Miller told IndieWire. “With Alice in particular, she wears this impractical, tight, fitted skirt suit. For me, that was always indicative of the way she is trying to control everything around her, including herself. Even the way she does her hair, she is trying to make sure that her world is safe and contained.”

But the world isn’t safe or containable, and that’s part of the character design, too. Billie doesn’t just have a sparkle in her eyes — he has a crescent moon, hinting at the importance she may hold in completing Hexe’s magic.

“The crescent moon was something that was done in Vis Dev, and then the lighting department told us, ‘We can track that all the way through,” Veerasunthorn told IndieWire. “[It hints at] something special and witchy about Billie, even though she doesn’t know that about herself yet. The way that you see her hair curled in the same shape of the crescent moon, too, is speaking to someone who is looking to fulfill her potential.”

Billie’s design, from the reflection of the moon in her eyes to the color and shape of her hair to the natural elements woven into her clothes, hints at her tendency toward witchiness — and toward belonging in a world she doesn’t even know she belongs in. “We as the audience, we can be like, ‘Girl, figure yourself out!’” Veerasunthorn joked.

Both Billie and Alice are designed in stark contrast to Celeste, who perhaps has too much figured out in terms of witch magic and her silvery, flowing, regal appearance. “[Celeste’s] magic is elegant and powerful, very controlled,” Veerasunthorn said. “The color of Alice’s magic is in between these two extremes, and we wanted to get the sense that there’s something broken about her magic that we don’t quite understand yet. There’s a lost-and-found quality, and hopefully subconsciously we’re hoping that she can put her magic back together.”

“What was a challenge was that it’s this world of magic, a world of witches, and we’ve seen that a lot in media,” Trinidad told IndieWire. “We were trying to find our unique take on that world and how we could be modern and fresh and also sort of pay homage to our own Disney legacy.”

One key way “Hexed” speaks to that Disney tradition is by having a powerful queen who blurs the line between what’s best for her and what’s best for the world. Celeste is also [SPOILER] Alice’s mother and Billie grandmother; there’s a long and proud Disney tradition of very complicated abuelas to outright villain grandmothers, which Bush himself has contributed to in the past.

“The worst part is that my own mother, who’s absolutely lovely, is a grandmother now to my three boys, and she is deeply offended by my choices,” Bush joked to IndieWire about what he has against grandmothers, anyway. “I think the only grandma I’ve written that’s been undeniably loving nonstop is Grandma Tala [from ‘Moana’] — and she didn’t survive the movie.”

But Celeste is a collection of influences from the writers’ lives, the Disney storytelling tradition, and wider pop culture — and not least the actor who ended up voicing her. “We were trying to figure [Celeste] out, and the second that Jodie said yes to the role, it changed the entire character. Because, to be honest, when you’re writing for Jodie Foster, that’s nerve-wracking,” Bush said. “We better get this right. We better make this character interesting and layered.”

Bush and Miller’s writing intended to create space between Celeste’s polished appearance and the roiling jealousy and insecurity she’s buried underneath. “She’s a real villain in a way that’s icky and, for me, that’s a really fun thing to write. On top of the fact that she’s this person trying to take power and maintain power any way that she can, she’s also weirdly vulnerable and needy at the same time. It’s this really uncomfortable combination of characteristics that was really fun to write and to see what Jodie would do with it.”

Leaving space in the writing for animation and performance, the collaboration between story and animation teams is a core part of the writing for “Hexed” and all other Disney Animation Studios films. “We sit down with our story artists and with our animators, and we say, for instance, ‘the premise is we’re going to a weird place with a bunch of reject familiars. What could happen there?’ And everyone spitballs, and great ideas rise to the surface,” Bush said. “More than anything, what I love doing is trying to find a fun sandbox and then being really willing to go wherever the great ideas go.”

Bush, Miller, Veerasunthorn, Trinidad, and Hand all told IndieWire that this openness to great ideas is what makes Disney animation so special, and can make even familiar storytelling territory feel fresh and exciting.

“Maybe we’re coming for granddads next,” Bush said.

#3453. PS5s Are in Short Supply for Black Friday, but You Can Still Buy One

There may be a ton of Black Friday deals on electronics, toys, and gadgets out there, but don't get your hopes up if you're looking for a PlayStation 5. Not only are they not discounted, but the combination of international chip shortages, high demand caused by the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, and the general holiday shopping frenzy has also made it nearly impossible to purchase a new, unbundled PlayStation 5 at any price—nearly impossible, but not impossible.

Whether you're looking for a PlayStation 5 Digital Edition, a PS5 with a disc drive, or the flagship PlayStation 5 Pro, you won't find them at major online retailers. PlayStation Direct lists all three consoles as "currently unavailable." Best Buy suggests making an account with them to "improve your odds" of getting one. I can't find a listing for a new PS5 on Amazon either.

You still have some options for obtaining a PS5, but none of them are great. Many refurbished PS5s are selling for well above the list price of a new unit. There are some bundled, special editions available, but you'll likely be paying a ton for those. If you're willing to get your hands dirty by dealing with the wild west of Facebook Marketplace, you might be able to track down a used PlayStation 5 at a reasonable price, but approach with extreme caution.

If you're looking for a refurbished PlayStation 5, the best way to avoid a headache is to focus on who did the refurbishing. Buying refurbished electronics directly from a manufacturer is generally safer than buying from a third party, and in this case, it's cheaper too. PlayStation Direct is offering a "Certified Refurbished PlayStation 5 Console" for the relatively reasonable price of $519, while a refurbished Slim sells for $499. But if you're in the market, I'd lock it in quick: PlayStation Direct is already out of refurbished PS5 Pros.

Amazon's Renewed program has some strict requirements for third parties to stay in the program, like keeping defect rates under 0.8%, but refurbished PlayStation 5s are going for a premium on Amazon at the moment. A quick look at the site reveals that the price of a refurbished PlayStation 5 is hovering near $900; a refurbished PS5 Slim will run you somewhere around $750, and the current average price of a refurbished PS5 Pro has ballooned to over $1,700. These are well above the retail prices of $649 for the standard version, $599 for the digital version, and $899 for the flagship Pro version of the PlayStation 5.

There are some bundled versions of the console listed for sale online too. If you buy one of these, you're getting a new console and some other piece of hardware or a game, but there's a ton of upcharge at the moment. They're generally more expensive than the original price and more expensive than refurbished units as well. Here are some examples:

Best Buy lists this PS5 Pro with PlayStation Portal Remote for $2,134.99.

GameStop lists a Ghost of Yotei Gold Limited Edition PS5 bundle for $769.99 ($731.49 for GameStop Pros).

Best Buy lists a PS5 Slim with an external drive for $979.99.

By far the largest used market for anything in the U.S. is Facebook Marketplace, including PlayStation 5s. I checked out my local Marketplace, and there are a lot of listings for the console within a 40-mile radius of Los Angeles. The average price of used PS5 consoles here is hovering between $300 and $500, which seems fairly reasonable. But with Facebook Marketplace, the number of potential red flags rises with the demand for the product.

I've bought and sold a fair number of things on Marketplace with no problems beyond the occasional flaky person, and I've written a list of hacks for the service, but I wasn't covering a "shortage buying" situation like this. Scams tend to rise with demand, so when I see a listing for a $150 PS5 console (that contains the text "$250 or best offer"), I'm suspicious. It could have been posted by someone who doesn't know what they have, but I wouldn't count on it. If you're buying a PS5 on Marketplace, check the model and generation details very carefully against the actual item. Make sure the seller is offering what you want and not a PlayStation 4 with PS5 games. Verify how it was stored and the condition it's in. But it ultimately can come down to vibes: Don't let your desire to score a PlayStation 5 get in the way of your gut check about the seller or situation.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

#3452. KPop Demon Hunter's Criterion Release Is The Best Argument For Home Media

Kpop Demon Hunters remains one of the defining films of its era. Released last year to strong reviews and a rapturous reception by general audiences, the movie (and its soundtrack) quickly became pop culture fixtures on a global scale. The sequel is currently in development, with worldwide musical tours set to keep love for the film thriving for years to come.

The fact that the movie launched on Netflix is part of that success, with the streaming service being a perfect place for fans to watch and rewatch the film to their heart's content. However, there's always been something about the movie that separated it from most original films that debut on the service. In fact, that sense of scale is a big reason why it connected so well.

It's also why Kpop Demon Hunters makes perfect sense as a Criterion Collection release. The movie never felt right constrained to a purely online experience, with the home release highlighting the craft and care that went into the movie through a lot of exclusive additions. It's a perfect addition to the Collection and a terrific showcase for why home media still has a place in the modern movie marketplace.

Kpop Demon Hunters is the rare film that launched on a streaming service that feels like it wasn't necessarily made for that kind of platform. Entering development in 2018, the film was formally added to the Sony Pictures Animation slate, with likely intentions to bring it the big screen.

In 2023, the film was formally added to the Netflix film slate as part of a collaborative deal between the studio and the streamer, eventually launching on the streaming service in 2025. Unlike a lot of other films released for streaming that are criticized for their limited scope and specific scale, Kpop Demon Hunters has a larger-than-life quality that's befitting the biggest screen possible.

Beyond the impressive visuals and tight action, the unifying vibes that come with the film's narrative and music make it the ideal movie to watch with larger groups. That's evidenced by the massive success the film has found in its short theatrical runs, which elicited surprisingly robust box office returns.

While the film's streaming release definitely contributed to its massive success - being able to rewatch it at leisure and throw impromptu watch parties gave the film a lot more legs than it might have otherwise - the film's true strength is that it feels genuinely epic. The fights have a showy quality that hides a lot of depth, while the musical numbers and visual gags have plenty to deconstruct.

The vibrancy of the animation makes it stand out from other films, coupled with the character design and sense of motion lends, it an anime-influenced tenor that feels wholly unique. It's a painfully unique film that feels deeply authentic to South Korean culture, without ever sacrificing its larger-than-life qualities for that grounding touch.

More than anything, Kpop Demon Hunters avoids the kind of repetitive dialogue and basic plot beats that many streaming movies are criticized for. While there are plenty of great movies released directly for streaming, there's often a sense of contained focus to those films that reflects the streaming model and set-up.

They need to be simple enough to have on in the background, when the best movies are the ones that command attention. Kpop Demon Hunters proves that a streaming service film can still have that sense of scale to feel like an entirely different world, all while still being grounded with character and comedy.

It feels like the kind of movie that only comes about because of years of craft and a lifetime's worth of passion. Streaming is great for audiences, but it's nice to see a movie launch on a platform that feels like so much more than what audiences have come to expect from those kinds of debuts.

All of the craft that went into the film can be overlooked on streaming services, which benefit from being able to give audiences a non-stop amount of content to fall into. However, that's where the likes of the Criterion Collection come into play. The distribution company has always been dedicated to elevating movie releases, showcasing the full depth of the filmmaking process that goes into every release.

The KPop Demon Hunters Criterion release is no different, with the kind of detailed additional elements that Netflix simply can't put alongside the film. The release contains a feature-length animatic for the film, highlighting its earliest complete setup. It includes a making-of documentary as well as video essays, focused on the artistic intention behind the film and the impact it has had on audiences.

It's the sort of thing home releases for films have that streaming just can't match. It's the kind of material that super fans and cinema nerds can dive into, gaining a fuller appreciation for the movie and everything going on behind the scenes. Movies like KPop Demon Hunters deserve that kind of showcase, not just because of the craft that went into it, but because of how much love the film has garnered since it came out.

It's the kind of attention that streaming just isn't designed for. In an era where home media is increasingly being phased out in favor of digital-only platforms, stuff like the Criterion Collection highlights what home media can offer that streamers simply can't. For film aficionados and die-hard fans alike, the Criterion Collection release of KPop Demon Hunters is a perfect addition to a personal library.

#3451. Anthropic launches new Claude Ship feature for builders

Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”

Claude Ship is a new product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding.

“That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic says. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic says.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic says.

You can learn much more about Claude Ship here. Additional documentation can be found here.

#3450. The Hunger Games Movies Are Officially Being Eliminated From Free Streaming

The Hunger Games' sixth installment, Sunrise on the Reaping, isout, and it’s already a certified hit. The Francis Lawrence-directed dystopian drama takes fans back to the 50th Hunger Games, where sixteen-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) is taking part in the games. The 67% Rotten Tomatoes-rated feature is being hailed for its performances and visual direction, while fans rated it even higher at 94%. It has earned $253.2 million worldwide on a $150 million budget, making it a commercial and critical success. After The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, a prequel following a young Coriolanus Snow, the latest feature has brought the franchise back to its box office dominance era.

The Hunger Games franchise started back in the 2000s, capitalizing on the viewers’ interest in the YA fantasy genre, which also includes the likes of Harry Potter, The Twilight Saga, and The Chronicles of Narnia. What distinguishes the Hunger Games franchise from its peers is the world-building where class divide, disparity, and an authoritarian system reign supreme. The themes of media manipulation, propaganda, violence as spectacle, and the cost of war, among others, resonated with fans worldwide. Resulting in the four movies collectively grossing approximately $2.97 billion worldwide. Fans who’d love to revisit the future, buckle up as the Hunger Games franchise, including The Ballad of Songbird and Snakes, is soon leaving free platform Tubi at the end of November.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Adapted from Suzanne Collins' novel trilogy of the same name, in The Hunger Games, we follow District 12 teenager Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), who volunteers to take her sister’s place in the upcoming games, surviving alongside fellow tribute Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson). With her win, she sparks nationwide defiance against the Capitol. In Catching Fire, President Snow (Donald Sutherland) forces past victors back into a deadly 75th Quarter Quell arena, where underground rebels rescue Katniss.

Like Harry Potter, the final book was divided into two movies. Mockingjay – Part 1 sees Katniss become the propaganda symbol of the revolution while rescuing a brainwashed Peeta from the Capitol. Finally, in Mockingjay – Part 2, full-scale war engulfs the Capitol. Katniss assassinates both Snow's regime and manipulative rebel leader Alma Coin (Julianne Moore), dismantling tyranny before returning home to build a peaceful life. The franchise has an illustrious cast including Liam Hemsworth, Woody Harrelson, Elizabeth Banks, Stanley Tucci, and more.

Check out The Hunger Games franchise before it leaves the platform on November 30. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3449. ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face

”The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” stands on its own as a beautifully written (by Quentin Tarantino) and directed (by David Fincher) Los Angeles noir that both invites and earns comparison with 1970s classics like “Night Moves” and “The Long Goodbye,” but its rewards increase exponentially the more familiar you are with its predecessor, “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Although Fincher and Tarantino have both argued that the movie is less a sequel than simply another Cliff Booth adventure, the movie has quite a few fun Easter eggs to reward fans of Brad Pitt’s first time playing the laid-back stuntman.

Perhaps the most delightful callback to “Once Upon a Time” is the reappearance of two of cowboy actor Rick Dalton’s (Leonardo DiCaprio) collaborators on the “Lancer” pilot that took up a good section of the middle third of Tarantino’s earlier film. Co-star James Stacy (Timothy Olyphant) makes a brief appearance alongside “Lancer” director Sam Wanamaker, played once again by Nicholas Hammond, whose exuberant turn as the real-life actor-director in “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” was one of that film’s greatest pleasures. Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

Hammond’s part is, like the other returning faces from “Once Upon a Time” (aside from Pitt, of course), essentially a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it cameo, but he was delighted to return to Tarantino’s world and to share the screen with Olyphant once again. He first heard rumblings that Wanamaker might return for “Cliff Booth” well over a year ago, when the assumption was that Tarantino would direct the script.

“Quentin has his team, and it’s the same crew that works on all his films,” Hammond told IndieWire. “I’d gotten to know them on ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,’ and a couple of the guys from the crew sent me emails saying, ‘Hey, it’s great we’re going to be working together again.’ Everyone had an ironclad NDA, so no one could tell me anything about the film, but that was my one little clue. Then, of course, when Quentin dropped out, and it looked like the movie was not happening, I thought, ‘There goes that chance.'”

Hammond was elated, therefore, when Pitt resurrected the movie by giving the script to his friend Fincher. “Timothy and I knew that we were coming in basically as an Easter egg,” Hammond said. “It was a tiny scene, and we knew that, but we were just thrilled that we were asked to come back, that Quentin thought it would be cool to have those characters back in the movie again. Let’s face it, he can get any actor he wants in the world to do anything, so it was an honor and a joy even though it’s a tiny little moment in the film.”

When Hammond played Wanamaker in the first film, he saw an opportunity to pay tribute to all the talented, hardworking directors and actors who work in the industry without necessarily becoming A-list names — a category that includes himself. “Your career ebbs and flows,” Hammond said. “You do a lot of small roles on television or small roles in movies, and then you get your own series, or then you get a big movie, and that’s the life of most actors in Hollywood. Even people like Leonardo and Brad say they have tons of friends who were as good as them when they were all starting out, but so much of it depends on if the right role comes along at the right moment.”

Hammond noted that for a lot of actors that moment never comes, but Tarantino has always recognized that that doesn’t make someone any less of an actor. “Most people think that if you’re good, you’re going to become a star. Quentin realizes there are a hell of a lot of very good actors out there who don’t become stars — that there are so many stars that have to align in the universe for that to happen. He admires and celebrates actors like Michael Madsen and Bruce Dern who have been journeyman actors their entire lives with moments of success, or flares of global recognition.”

Hammond experienced one of those flares as a teenager, when he played one of the Von Trapp kids in Robert Wise’s classic musical “The Sound of Music,” and again several years later when he played Peter Parker on the CBS television series “The Amazing Spider-Man” — the role that made Tarantino a lifelong Hammond fan. “I’m fortunate in that way,” Hammond said. “I feel luckier than most actors in my situation, because I’ve had a few goalpost roles that the world is aware of.”

60 years after he made it, Hammond still runs into “Sound of Music” fans all the time. “I was on a plane yesterday flying to Sydney, and a stewardess crouched down next to my seat and said, ‘Nicholas, I just have to let you know that my family watches ‘Sound of Music’ every year,'” Hammond said. “‘When my grandmother was ready to pass away, she said the last thing she wanted was for all of us to gather around the TV together as a family and watch that movie.’ I don’t care how rich you are or how many movies you’ve been in, how many actors get a chance to be in a movie that has that kind of effect on people?”

Hammond says that, having lived through the eras “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” and “Cliff Booth” recreate, he knows Tarantino got that period of L.A. history completely right—something he attributes to the writer’s encyclopedic knowledge of his own work and that of all his peers. “There are very few people who could capture the 1970s as accurately as Quentin does,” Hammond said. “It’s his era. He grew up watching me as Peter Parker in ‘Spider-Man,’ and he watched all the episodes of ‘Gunsmoke’ I did, and all the episodes of ‘The Waltons’ and ‘The Brady Bunch.’ There’s not a show I was on that he didn’t see and know about.”

In “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” Hammond honored the directors of those episodic series whose names the public has forgotten, though Wanamaker, as an actor, was probably better known than many. When he got the part, Hammond was intent on playing Wanamaker with respect while still delivering on all the comic potential of Tarantino’s conception. “One of my fears when we were doing the film is I did not want Zoe Wanamaker to think we were making fun of her father, because we definitely weren’t,” Hammond said. “He was a very serious actor and a serious theater person.”

Hammond took a deep dive into Wanamaker’s life and career for the part. “Quentin’s office sent me a stack of DVDs of movies that Wanamaker had directed, and movies that he had appeared in,” Hammond said. “I got quite familiar with him. The Globe Theatre exists in England today solely because of him. If it weren’t for Sam Wanamaker petitioning and raising money and basically forcing the British government to authorize the building, the Globe wouldn’t be there. They wanted to build public housing there, and he managed to get a groundswell of support. And now, of course, it’s a huge tourist attraction, and in his honor the smaller studio theater within the building is called the Sam Wanamaker Theater.”

Hammond says he knew he was a part of something special when he saw “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” at its Cannes world premiere. “I’ve been lucky enough to be in three really significant films: [Peter Brook’s] ‘Lord of the Flies,’ ‘The Sound of Music,’ and ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,'” Hammond said. “With three very significant directors. So I’ve had a very fortunate career, and I still get excited just seeing my name on the call sheet. And when you’re working with people like Leo or Timothy Olyphant who are right at the top of their game, they’re the best of the best. I’m on the New York Yankees now, and when I get up to the plate, I better deliver.”

Despite starring in several classics, Hammond is less interested in looking back than in whatever he’s working on now. “I absolutely love being an actor, and I love being on stage. I’ve done a great deal of stage work, and I’m always asked, ‘Which do you like better?’ And the answer always is, whatever I’m doing right then. When I walk into the stage door of a theater, I get exactly the same charge of excitement that I do walking onto a sound stage at a studio. I just feel like I’m home. I feel these are my people. These are the people that I’ve always been the happiest being with since I was 10 years old, and I that will never change.”

Hammond looks to his “Sound of Music” costar Christopher Plummer, who did some of his best work late in life, as a role model. “I’ll do this as long as I possibly can. I’m of the Christopher Plummer philosophy that way,” Hammond said. “The word retirement doesn’t really exist. What would I do? Give up the thing I love the most in the world to play golf? I’m not doing that.”

#3445. 5 Near-Perfect Netflix Series With Less Than 20 Episodes

Netflix has a shaky history when it comes to keeping its best shows alive, given that the streamer has rarely renewed shows beyond a third season. While the obvious reason for this is a cynical justification of not wanting to give bonuses to writers, it does result in many shows that are either cut off before their prime or forced to reach their finales at too early a date.

The Netflix library is filled with shows that have a shorter number of overall episodes, but determining which ones are truly of value can be a challenging ordeal. While Netflix might not have the same consistent level of quality across all of its programming as rival streamers like HBO Max or Apple TV do, it nonetheless has produced exceptional television shows which left a sizable impact, regardless of how many episodes they had.

Mindhunter is a captivating true crime thriller from the brilliant filmmaker David Fincher, which is loosely based on FBI Agent John Douglas and his research into psychopathic killers in the 1970s, which helped to coin the phrase “serial killer.” The show follows the FBI investigators Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff) and Bill Tench (Holy McCallany) as they interview and profile some of the most famous killers in American history, all whilst helping local cops solve puzzling crimes.

Mindhunter is crafted with the same meticulous style that defines Fincher’s best work, while also offering deep subtext about the extent to which empathy can make someone vulnerable. While the show’s looming expenses and Fincher’s notoriously detail-oriented approach to capturing historical detail may have prevented Mindhunter from getting a third season, it remains one of the best things that Netflix has ever produced.

Bodyguard was a true phenomenon of a summer streaming sensation that became a massive hit in the United Kingdom on BBC during 2018 before making its American debut on Netflix, where it picked up even more steam. In only six episodes, Bodyguard offered an unforgettable mystery and served as a starmaking performance from Richard Madden in his first major role after his run as Robb Stark on Game of Thrones.

Bodyguard is more than just a murder mystery, as it works as a conspiracy thriller, a political drama, a dark romance, and a feat of non-stop action. There has been no shortage of spy shows released within the past decade on streaming, but Bodyguard is the rare instance of a series that operates with the scale of a studio blockbuster while offering the type of intimate interpersonal relationships that would only be fit for the small screen.

Midnight Mass is the crowning achievement of Mike Flanagan’s career and the most deeply idiosyncratic and personal work that he has ever made. While the two previous horror shows that Flanagan had made for Netflix succeeded in offering classical family drama within a gothic atmosphere, Midnight Mass is an equally gripping character study that goes to supremely dark places, including the type of graphic content that would have a hard time making it on any other streaming service.

The brilliance of Midnight Mass is that Flanagan weaves a historical understanding of the occult into a grounded story of religious fanaticism and the monopolization of fear, suggesting that the pandemonium that gripped the past is not entirely the stuff of legends. Hamish Linklater had already been a reliable character actor up to this point in time, but Midnight Mass turned him into a total icon within the horror community.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Lord of the Flies is not the first adaptation of the classic William Golding novel that is often taught in schools, but it is the most comprehensive interpretation of its dark coming-of-age story because the four-part series is divided between the perspectives of the four main characters: Ralph, Piggy, Simon, and Jack. While this version of Lord of the Flies is still set in the novel’s original setting of the 1950s, the freshness came from the writing by Jack Thorne, who had also created Adolescence.

Lord of the Flies captures the way that kids actually talk and act in a way that none of the previous adaptations have shown themselves capable of, but the empathy that extends to the entire cast of characters does not prevent the show from getting to the heart of Golding’s prophetic message about collapsing society.

Black Doves is the most bingeable spy show on the air right now because it takes a very different approach to the idea of former operatives being called out of retirement. Keira Knightley plays the wife of a politician who is placed in the middle of a conspiracy after her past as a covert assassin is threatened to be revealed, and Ben Whishaw is equally convincing as her former partner.

The first season of Black Doves is the perfect show to watch over the holidays because it is a straight shot of adrenaline that is set entirely over the Christmas season, and the second season was a major jump up in quality that raised the stakes while adding more character depth, action, and surprising humor. Although it has not yet been revealed whether the show will get a Season 3, the 12 episodes that exist are already riveting.

#3442. Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible

WETA FX has been called upon to do visual effects for everything, from orc armies to superheroes, alien planetscapes to the innards of a whale. On each project, they have to match the movie’s consistency. The goal is to make sure that the VFX blends perfectly into the overall visual style, not so unlike a certain Springfield dad creeping into a hedge.

Meeting that challenge often means the teams at WETA match and then build on live-action footage to get as close to a photorealistic look as possible. But adding digital effects to the wonderful world of stop-motion animation, as with “Wildwood,” WETA FX got to have more fun with creating a world that looks as textured and handmade as the puppets designed and animated by Laika Studios. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

“Everybody was super stoked about this film because it’s so different from what we usually do. People got to be artists,” VFX supervisor Sabine Laimer told IndieWire. “We’re really good at making effects invisible, but here we could actually showcase the artistry. All of our people here loved it.”

This applies to the way that WETA helped intensify battle sequences, the way they expanded sets so that they feel as fast as the impassible woods where most of “Wildwood” takes place, and the way they were able to match cinematographer Caleb Deschanel’s lighting to bring a unity to the digital and puppetry work within individual scenes. When designing the ivy that Alexandra (Carey Mulligan) seeks to control and that Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) seeks to pacify, WETA’s digital leaves weren’t meant to mimic real leaves in nature. They were built to look like the paper leaves a stop motion animator would use.

“[The leaves in ‘Wildwood’] have a different light transmission. They have a different level of detail, depending on how close the camera is to them,” Laimer said. “[We developed] this sort of stage realism, if you want to call it that, rather than realism, and that makes a huge difference.”

One element where WETA needed to heighten the realism most was the ivy, which is eventually summoned into a sentient spire that threatens to overwhelm the entire world. “It’s alive, but it’s not a person. It has character, but it can’t feel like it’s a boss. It has to have intent, but it can’t be so direct that it feels like there’s a brain that’s going after the characters,” VFX supervisor Dan Macarin laid out the challenge of Laika’s brief to IndieWire.

“It had to creep, it had to attack, it had to consume, it had to overgrow,” Laimer added. “There was a lot of material there for us to work with, which was amazing, but we had to translate all of this intricate detail that they’ve built on their practical sets into a digital plinth environment and build it in a way that was malleable for us, and we had different stages of everything.”

Laimer and her team tested ways to mimic the Laika animators’ practical work and drew inspiration from the natural world, like time-lapses of pea shoots with an uncanny, jerky motion as they grow. They built different vignettes that could be placed inside specific shots so the ivy would read as dangerous, but not distract from the drama between the characters. For the moments where the ivy threatens to overwhelm the entire plinth, the WETA team actually used fluid simulation to get the feel of the ivy being like a tsunami, this swelling of constant, growing motion that is headed in a definite direction, not just moving at random.

“We looked at practical references like schools of fish, where they move in unison and create shapes and change directions on purpose. It was a similar thing, or like flocks of starlings in the air. You have to sculpt the [ivy] cyclone per shot so that it’s not distracting in the background, it’s not too busy, but at the same time still feels like it’s alive,” Laimer said.

Hitting that visual effects sweet spot was important in all the visual effects collaborations between WETA and Laika. The path to do that always ran through story, and what visuals would make the storytelling the most immediately legible to the audience. “WETA is really, really fantastic at doing third act battles,” Macarin said. “We’ve done a tremendous number of them over the years and decades, and so it’s not the scope that we have to worry about. We can handle all of that. It’s always, ‘How do we tell this story?’”

In the case of “Wildwood,” telling the story with visual effects meant simplifying a lot, so that even when we placed it behind the explosion of cannon fire (where it would never be safe for a practical camera to go), we still cared about the characters. “We were able to create aesthetic choices that still allow the audience to engage in the battle, but not necessarily put you suddenly into this photorealistic explosion or feel. This is a very colorful, emotionally driven sequence that just happens to have a battle around it,” Macarin said.

The most fantastical-seeming choices in “Wildwood” are all about character. “They shot everything with two suns,” Laimer said. “They had a smaller, sharper key light and then a softer, wider one, which created this really beautiful falloff on the faces that we had to create digitally. That was really cool.”

Getting to build expressive, beautiful worlds in animation — whether digital, stop-motion, or a combination of the two — usually is pretty cool, to be fair. And clearly, in the case of “Wildwood,” it brings out some of WETA’s best work.

#3440. Heat Meets Ocean's 11 In Apple TV's New Thriller Series Releasing Through Christmas

There's a new thriller on Apple TV that's a little bit Ocean's Eleven, a little bit Heat, and it's releasing over Christmas for those looking for a new holiday watch. Apple TV has become a streamer for must-watch television. It's a long way from its beginnings, marked by plenty of missteps.

Now, Apple TV is reaching the HBO level, where you can hear that a show is coming to Apple, and just by virtue of being on the streamer, it's likely worth watching. Speaking of which, there's a new heist thriller series that began airing on Apple TV on November 13, 2026, with a finale set for December 25, 2026.

12 12 12 is the latest thriller series on Apple TV, and it combines the cat-and-mouse game from the point of view of the thief and the police, like Heat, while also featuring a creative, ensemble heist, just like in Ocean's Eleven. This 8-episode series comes from Dudi Appleton and Jim Keeble.

Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan star as FBI Special Agent Jack Strickland and Paul Galvin, respectively. Paul is a renowned criminal and thief who Jack believes is responsible for the death of his partner. When Paul goes for one last heist in Zurich, Jack will do just about anything to apprehend him.

12 12 12 currently has a 59% on Rotten Tomatoes, probably not what the showrunners were hoping for. Most critics agree that the show gets going towards the latter half of the series, as the end stage of the heist is shown and the final part of Jack's hunt for the criminals is revealed, but there's some disagreement about whether the journey there is worth it.

The shifting timelines and three-act approach do seem to offer a unique take on a fairly standard storyline. For others, it only made things more unnecessarily complex and confusing. The large ensemble cast that changes in between storylines also does help the chaotic nature of the show.

The unique title of 12 12 12 comes from the FBI's Principles of Crime, which states that, for a high-asset robbery, like the one Paul pulls off in Zurich, it takes 12 months of planning, 12 hours to actually do the heist, and then the police have 12 days to solve it. 12 12 12's audience is reminded of this at the top of every episode.

Furthermore, each episode is broken up into three distinct sections. One part takes place during the planning stage, another during the heist, and the next during the hunt. What we learn in each section informs what we learn in the next, and sometimes, information is revealed that changes the way we understand what we've already seen.

12 12 12 is a fairly straightforward heist show, and while the three-timeline approach is somewhat novel, it's not actually all that different from a story that fans of the heist genre will be familiar with. There's a thief trying to leave the criminal life but is forced back in for one last job, and a bitter detective who needs to catch him.

What will determine whether you'll like the show or not will probably have to do with your relationship with the two leads, Mackie and Dornan. They're both doing fine, capable work, and anytime they're on screen 12 12 12 is better for it. If those two actors don't particularly interest you, you might be better off watching Heat or Ocean's Eleven.

#3438. The 10 Greatest Rock Albums of the '60s, Ranked

The '60s was a hugely important era for rock music – perhaps the most important decade for the progression of the genre. Folk and protest influences were abundant, and the British Invasion was globalizing the genre. The counterculture was in full swing, bringing a psychedelic edge to rock and roll. The world was in a state of constant transformation, and the music of the decade mirrored this relentless change. Musicians began to experiment like they never had before, pushing the boundaries of what was possible – and what was socially acceptable. There was so much variety and innovation during this time that picking the top ten rock albums of the 1960s may seem like an impossible task. And, yet, here they are.

The second album from chaotic British rock band Cream definitely made an impact. An incredible amount of creativity and experimentation was packed into these eleven songs (clocking in at a mere 33 minutes.) Both of the singles released ahead of this album — “Strange Brew” and “Sunshine of Your Love” — charted in the UK, and the latter made it to number five in the US. Disraeli Gears bridged the gap between their earlier blues rock sound with the psychedelic tint they later took on. Perhaps “earlier” and “later” are the wrong words – the band dissolved after only three years together due to irreconcilable differences between bassist Jack Bruce and live-wire drummer Ginger Baker.

Willy and The Poor Boys by Creedence Clearwater Revival is about as far as you can get from the psychedelic rock wave taking over the UK and the US. This album is straight up Americana swamp-rock. The narrative storytelling and the focus on the American middle class make this album a stand-out and a fan favorite. The record was initially supposed to be a concept album, written and recorded from the perspective of fictional jug band Willy and The Poor Boys. While they didn’t end up following through with this idea, some of the texture remained – the story of the jug band that never was is expressed through the popular track “Down on the Corner.”

Led Zeppelin II is widely considered to be the band's heaviest album. Their music style was evolving as the '60s slipped into the '70s – they were reshaping traditional American blues music into something with much more firepower. This album included three covers of Chicago-based blues songs and six original tracks. It was written while Led Zeppelin was on tour, recorded in myriad studios and cities (and even on Jimmy Page’s houseboat!) This constant relocation added to the chaotic feel of the album. But despite the constant motion, Zeppelin II comes together as a cohesive record, featuring dynamic shifts in volume and tone, driving guitar, and musical (rather than lyrical) hooks.

Electric Ladyland is the third and final album from the Jimi Hendrix Experience. The record initially confounded critics – they weren’t sure whether to love or hate the trippy, immersive, funky acid rock album Hendrix had created. It was an unprecedented piece of work, so some confusion is understandable. Nowadays, the record is regarded as one of the greatest albums in rock and roll. Hendrix referred to these songs as "sound paintings,” which is abundantly evident in the album. Each track is layered and ambient, drawing the listener deep into a bottomless well of sound. And lest we forget – this album also includes Hendrix’s legendary reinterpretation of Bob Dylan’s “All Along the Watchtower.”

Jim Morrison and The Doors were a darker voice in the 1960s counterculture. On their self-titled debut album, the group mixes poetry, blues, psychedelia, and experimentation to create an incredibly important record. This record was developed through live performances, mostly at LA’s iconic venue Whiskey a Go Go. They released their single “Light My Fire” ahead of the album, which quickly got the public interested in their music. The Doors had an inconceivable impact on the bands that came after them, across a wide array of genres. Alternative rock and punk would not be what they are today without the music of The Doors.

What's a rock and roll list without The Rolling Stones? Their eighth studio album Let It Bleed is a return to their earlier blues, gospel, and hard rock sound. The record was also heavily inspired by American roots music and the overwhelming feeling of disillusionment much of the Western world experienced throughout the 1960s. Let It Bleed includes some of their biggest hits to date, such as “Gimme Shelter” and “You Can’t Always Get What You Want.” Throughout the writing and recording of this album, the band was in a time of intense turmoil. Founding member and guitarist Brian Jones was slipping deeper into addiction and failing to show up for rehearsals, resulting in his termination from the group. He tragically passed away a few weeks later. He was replaced by Mick Taylor, and both musicians appear on the album. Keith Richards had to pick up a lot of the slack in the string section, which permanently altered the band’s sound. The release of Let It Bleed ushered in the band’s most successful period.

Tommy by The Who took six months to write and record — an unusually long period for bands at this time. This extended interval was well worth it, producing an iconic and unprecedented concept album. It would be impossible to rush the complex storytelling, theatricality, and groundbreaking scale of the record. Tommy, written by guitarist Pete Townshend, was the first album to be labeled a "rock opera". Townshend was inspired by Indian spiritual practices. The album follows the fictional Tommy Walker through his life, which is plagued by murder, abuse, and drugs. Tommy overcomes these myriad hardships to eventually become a messiah figure and spiritual leader. Tommy is widely considered to be The Who’s breakout album.

Highway 61 Revisited is Bob Dylan’s sixth studio album. In this body of work, we see Dylan depart further from folk music, incorporating an increasing number of rock musicians in the studio. This album is in many ways a continuation of his 1965 record Bringing It All Back Home. Dylan’s poetic lyrics capture the political and cultural unrest of America in the midst of the Vietnam War. His lyrics are steeped in clever allegory and impressionism, buoyed by a relentless blues-rock drive. With each album release, Dylan’s energy and rebellion grows.

The Velvet Underground & Nico was greatly underappreciated during the time of its release. It is the band’s debut album, a collaboration with German model and singer Nico, a partnership that was carefully engineered by artist Andy Warhol. The record tackled unconventional and controversial subject matter like drugs and sadomasochism, which shocked the public — it was banned from many radio stations and record stores. The Velvet Underground’s avant-garde, abrasive sound did well in New York City’s underground scene, but pretty much nowhere else. They were well before their time, setting the stage for punk, alternative, and psychedelic rock. Many consider it to be the original art rock record. Today, it is finally appreciated for the masterpiece that it truly is.

The Beatles’ Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band is a landmark psychedelic rock album – perhaps the most important body of work to come from the 1960s. This record was a huge moment in popular culture and helped to define the Summer of Love. It is an early example of a concept album, wildly innovative in every aspect of creation and production. The album is based upon a fictional band conceptualized by Paul McCartney and includes a vast array of whimsical and unusual influences, including vaudeville and circus music. This incredible album set the stage for prog rock and countless other genres, changing the face of rock and popular music forever.

#3436. ‘Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema Was More Interested in the Intimate Than the Epic

Christopher Nolan‘s adaptation of Homer’s “The Odyssey” was one of the most awe-inspiring cinematic achievements of 2026, an epic worthy of comparison with the grandiose visions of David Lean and Stanley Kubrick. Yet what interested cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema was less the story’s vast scale than the details of the human faces inhabiting the film‘s sweeping vistas.

“We never really treated it in an epic way,” van Hoytema told IndieWire. “Even though we all know ‘The Odyssey‘ and understand the scale of the story, making some sort of a tourist film was never on our agenda. It was the characters and the visceral sense of their experience that we were interested in, so even standing in the most crazy places in the world — on mountaintops or wherever — we were never motivated by the landscapes. The settings take care of creating the scale and scope of the film — our perspective on the story was a very intimate one.” Related Stories Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face

Given that, van Hoytema tried not to be seduced by the beauty of his surroundings if it didn’t serve the emotional experience. “It was less about showing how beautiful a beach was than about showing how shitty those men felt when they were on the beach,” he said, noting that a key tool in getting across the characters’ internal feelings was shooting the film entirely in IMAX.

“Shooting an entire film in IMAX has been a pursuit of ours for quite a long time now, and we’ve been tweaking the lenses and tweaking the cameras in order to get there,” van Hoytema said. “We’ve managed to wrangle the equipment and technology around it to enable us to be right there next to you, looking straight into your eyes.”

This again plays into that idea of intimacy versus scale, which was something van Hoytema and Nolan had experimented with in “Oppenheimer.” In that film, IMAX was used not only for major set pieces like the atomic bomb test, but quiet dialogue scenes shot largely in close-up. Van Hoytema says that he and Nolan have long been aware that IMAX has historically been used mostly to depict the wonders of the world, but they wanted to expand its grammar.

“The lenses that we use today are an evolution of different iterations of lenses that we have been building through the years, lenses that focus extremely close and that can open wide so that you can work with natural light or in half-darkness,” van Hoytema said. “We’ve found that IMAX is an intimate format because it’s such a good replicator of the human experience and perspective.”

The biggest obstacle toward shooting an entire movie in IMAX before “The Odyssey” was always the sound — IMAX film cameras are famously noisy, making it difficult to get decent production recordings. “We built a blimp on ‘Tenet,’ but it didn’t work,” van Hoytema said. “This was the first film where we felt that the technology had gotten far enough to actually shoot the entire thing on IMAX. There’s been an evolution in development not only in my department but in the sound department — they have come up with better microphones, better filtration, and in this film it came together beautifully.”

Van Hoytema and Nolan always had a backup plan in case the IMAX cameras became too unwieldy or got in the way of performance, particularly in lengthy dialogue scenes that would outlast the cameras’ short magazines. Once Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway proved that they could pull off a complicated sequence in close collaboration with van Hoytema and the other departments, however, Nolan and his crew were confident they could rely on IMAX as their format of choice. “That day was the hardest, and we shot everything on IMAX, so for the rest of the film we just committed — no plan B,” van Hoytema said.

While van Hoytema and Nolan were enthusiastic about committing to IMAX, it did create massive logistical challenges — not just when it came to getting the heavy camera and blimp in and out of remote locations, but in terms of performance. The actors’ eyelines, for example, were often blocked by the enormous camera. “Here we are bragging about the intimacy we can achieve, and suddenly you’re on set with a gigantic black box in front of the actors, and they can’t look each other in the eyes,” van Hoytema said. “It was a huge problem.”

To solve the problem, van Hoytema and his crew built a system that would allow the actors to see each other. “It was based on a teleprompter that has an angled mirror in front of the lens, and people can look straight into the lens reading a teleprompter because it has projected text on it. But instead of text, we had another mirror, and we had an actor sitting here. So basically what actors see is a little surface with a mirror with the other actor in there, and they can look straight into the other actor’s eye.”

Van Hoytema could fine-tune the eyelines by adjusting the angles of the mirrors in what he called “a very analog but very effective solution. And the actors loved it, because instead of looking at a wall they’re literally looking at their co-stars.” Van Hoytema reiterated the idea that everything in the movie was geared toward character and performance — including, at times, making the actors as uncomfortable as possible.

“It’s not for nothing that Chris loves to go out at sea with a ship and do things that are almost physically impossible,” van Hoytema said. “The more miserable or real or wet the situation is, the more the actors have to react to and play with. And that also goes for my way of working. I love different weather situations. I love different light situations. I love kinetic and physical challenges. It adds something unexpected and something visceral. The camera’s always fighting something and the actors are fighting at that very same moment, so it becomes a weirdly symbiotic relationship to the elements.”

In spite — or perhaps because — of the arduous shoot, van Hoytema didn’t want to see it end. “This was an extremely difficult film, but it was also the film where everything we’d been working toward came together,” van Hoytema. “We were much more light-footed. Weirdly enough, when what you’re doing becomes subjected to elements that you cannot control, you become a bit less precious. And that lack of preciousness is very liberating. We just went in headfirst.”
