#3435. 8 Live-Action Transformers Designs That Are 10/10 Perfect

Across the entire live-action Transformers franchise, there are just some designs that will never be beaten. Without a doubt, Michael Bay changed the game in 2007 with the start of his live-action series, breathing new life into the entire Transformers franchise as a whole. Part of that includes some of the raddest live-action robots to ever be seen on the big-screen.

Since the 80s and the original animated series, characters like Optimus Prime, Bumblebee, and Megatron have had very distinct looks both in animation and as physical toys. As a result, translating those iconic depictions to live-action was always going to be one of the biggest hurdles to getting audiences on board. That said, very few live-action Transformers designs look bad, and a select few have certainly achieved GOAT-status.

Keeping that in mind, here are 8 of the most perfect, 10/10 live-action Transformers designs we absolutely love, based on pure cool factor, unique appearances that just work, and/or excellent live-action translations.

Without question, Devastator is one of the most ambitious and intimidating designs in the live-action Transformers franchise, largely due to the sheer scale of the massive Decepticon. Formed from six different Constructicons (just like in the original animated series), Devastator is a huge Combiner who debuted in 2009's Revenge of the Fallen, deployed by Megatron in Egypt to uncover the giant Star Harvester hidden within the Great Pyramid of Giza.

Rather than combining from construction vehicles that are all the same green-and-purple color, each piece of Devastator is mismatched with various colors, along with a gaping maw of a mouth and multiple eyes. As such, the industrial monster that is Devastator has one of the scariest and most intimidating live-action Decepticon designs, despite his limited screen time in the Transformers franchise.

Also debuting in Revenge of the Fallen, Sideswipe is one of the sleekest Autobots in the live-action movies. Transforming into a silver Chevrolet Corvette Stingray, Sideswipe's most notable design feature in his robot form is two car wheels positioned as his feet like roller skates, allowing him to move across a battlefield with more fluid motion than most of his fellow Autobots. He also has large blades on his arms, making his distinct fighting style even more of a unique threat to the Decepticons.

Debuting in 2014's Age of Extinction, Crosshairs' chosen vehicle form is notably a later-model Chevrolet Corvette Stingray, having a shared vehicle form with Sideswipe in the earlier Transformers films, with a green color scheme rather than silver. However, what makes Crosshairs so awesome is that he arguably has one of the most stylish robot forms in the live-action Transformers franchise, having an effortlessly cool coat-like configuration of vehicle parts that very much adds to his gunslinger personality/aesthetic. Likewise, Crosshairs' dual pistols cement his role as an Autobot survivor/combat specialist.

Debuting in 2011's Dark of the Moon, Decepticon Shockwave has one of the coolest and most powerful designs in the live-action movies. Featuring a single eye just like his counterpart in the original animated series, the emotionless Shockwave on the big-screen commands his Driller pet, a huge Cybertronian beast made up of several devastatingly massive mechanical tentacles, making him one of the most formidable Decepticons in the entire franchise. While he doesn't receive nearly enough screen time in Dark of the Moon, Shockwave is easily one of the biggest and scariest threats.

Debuting in the first live-action Transformers movie, Michael Bay's Megatron design is more original compared to his more traditional, G1 look. However, the unique design eventually became iconic in its own right and is certainly one of the most intimidating and fearsome-looking versions of the Decepticon leader across the franchise.

Having an incredibly angular and pointed appearance with jagged edges, sharp teeth, and clawed hands, Megatron is the epitome of a deadly weapon brought to life. Capable of turning into both a brutal tank and alien jet in the live-action movies, the Bayverse Megatron is a prime example of a design that has major cool factor points, despite its more original appearance.

As a major caveat to this list, it has to be noted that the brief Cybertron flashbacks in 2018's Bumblebee feature some of the coolest G1-inspired live-action designs, quick as they are. While it seems unfair to the entire live-action franchise to simply list all the bots seen in just a couple of minutes of screen time, personal bias compels me to at least include Soundwave.

Unlike the version seen in 2011's Dark of the Moon, the version of Soundwave seen in Bumblebee embraces everything that made his original G1 so awesome, including his monotone vocoder voice, blue-and-gray color scheme with yellow accents and red eyes, shoulder cannon, and chest compartment to launch his various cassette minions like Ravage and Laserbeak. A perfect combination of classic G1 appearance with more modern detailing, Soundwave's design in 2018's Bumblebee is easily one of the coolest and most satisfying when it comes to the live-action Decepticons.

Now we get to Bumblebee himself, who's easily one of the most important bots in the entire Bayverse and beyond as Optimus Prime's loyal lieutenant who's also best friends with crucial human characters like Shia LaBeouf's Sam Witwicky and Hailee Steinfeld's Charlie Watson.

Bumblebee has gone through several different live-action designs with his classic yellow-and-black color scheme, starting with his epic Camaro vehicle forms that redefined the look of the character for a new generation of Transformers fans, complete with car-door "wings" on his back and a face shield with insectoid-like eyes to help add to his namesake. However, the classic Autobot's appearance in his 2018 solo movie arguably provides the best balance between G1 authenticity with a more classic 1967 Volkswagen Beetle vehicle form, while still keeping with the robot design established in the earlier Bayverse movies.

With slightly more rounded proportions thanks to his classic vehicle form, Bumblebee looks so good in his spin-off. However, that isn't to say he's ever looked bad in earlier movies or the Transformers films that followed with his truly awesome Camaro forms. Also, his expressive face does wonders for the character, who more often than not uses radio frequencies to speak to make up for his damaged voice. He's a true "heart of the franchise" character if ever there was one.

It shouldn't come as a huge surprise that Optimus Prime ranks at the top of this list. As the noble leader of the Autobots, Optimus has arguably received the most attention of any character in the entire live-action Transformers franchise, and for good reason. While he's had many different forms and designs over the years with varying levels of authenticity to the classic G1 look, you really can't go wrong with the OG live-action that debuted with Michael Bay's first film back in 2007.

Optimus Prime's live-action debut was a major cinematic achievement, translating his classic semi-truck appearance into a mechanical form that felt both practical and natural in "real life." Featuring red flames and accents on a blue frame, Optimus' OG form still holds classic features like his iconic face shield and distinct head design, while still having a more complex and modernized form to best convey how a truck could indeed transform its parts into a massive robot body in live-action.

Not every Optimus Prime form has been universally loved (The Last Knight's wasn't great), and more recent versions like the Optimus seen in Bumblebee and Rise of the Beasts have embraced G1 aesthetics even further, which has been cool to see. Nevertheless, the Bayverse's OG design is arguably still the best for live-action Optimus Prime, and the most perfect 10/10 design for the entire Transformers franchise overall. Without such a solid look and design for Transformers' most central character and hero, I sincerely doubt the franchise would have done as well as it has.

#3434. iOS 27.2 upgraded Apple Photos in two ways, here’s what’s new

Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27, but the recent release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new.

Shared Albums are among my favorite features in the Photos app. I don’t post on social media often, but I love using Shared Albums because they provide a social media-style experience in a private way that lives right inside Photos.

iOS 27 brought a variety of big improvements to Shared Albums. And in iOS 27.2, Apple introduced four more.

Per Apple’s release notes, here’s what’s new:

To get these new features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the issue with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software update adds the following:

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground

SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.

#3431. Apple Pay just got even better with four new features and more

Apple Pay is a go-to feature for iPhone users when shopping in stores, online, and in apps. Apple recently announced four new features that make Apple Pay even better. Here’s how they work, plus one major expansion that’s rolling out now.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

One of my favorite changes in iOS 27 is the redesigned Apple Pay checkout interface. The new interface makes it much easier to switch between different cards during the checkout flow on websites and in apps.

In the new design, you can easily swipe between cards on the main Apple Pay checkout screen. You can also tap on a card to view a grid of all your available Apple Pay cards.

The design also makes it easier to see information about individual cards, including rewards, balances, pay later options, and more.

iOS 27 was released to everyone last week. You can update in the Settings app on your iPhone.

Apple and American Express recently announced a new partnership that lets you pay with American Express rewards points.

When shopping online or in apps with an American Express card, you’ll see a new “Use Rewards” option alongside your available Membership Rewards points balance. You can apply points to cover all or part of your purchase, right in the Apple Pay checkout flow.

American Express points redeemed via Apple Pay are valued at 0.7 cents each. For example, this means 10,000 points can be redeemed for $70 applied towards your purchase.

In iOS 27, Apple is adding a new “Tap to Share” feature that integrates with Apple Pay on iPhone for in-store shopping.

This feature is an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone. Apple explains:

With just a tap, customers can connect to a participating merchant’s iPhone for a more personalized and faster in-store purchase experience that allows for secure sharing of information, such as email and other contact information, shipping address, loyalty rewards information, and more.

Customers will also be able to view the items in their basket in real time so they can keep track of what they’ve purchased and ensure all sales and discounts are properly applied.

When done, shoppers can complete the checkout on their iPhone using Apple Pay.

iPhone users with select banks can manage their debit card balances directly in the Apple Pay interface. According to Apple, you’ll be able to use Apple Pay to add money to a supported debit card directly in Apple Wallet or when checking out.

This one isn’t really a new feature developed by Apple. Instead, it’s something that should’ve happened years ago finally coming to fruition. Walmart has announced that it is finally starting to roll out support for Apple Pay. Apple Pay is also rolling out to Sam’s Club as part of this initiative.

As of November, Walmart’s roll out of Apple Pay across the United States is complete.

As Apple Pay continues to increase in popularity and prevalence among retailers, it’s great to see Apple continue to improve the experience. Personally, Apple Pay is my checkout payment method of choice basically everywhere I shop — whether that’s online or in store.

#3427. Forget The Lord of the Rings, These 4 Books Do Epic Fantasy Much Better

Back in 1937, J. R. R. Tolkien published The Hobbit. This children's high fantasy novel about a home-loving hobbit going on a grand adventure quickly became a critical and commercial success, and is still one of the bestselling books in history. That same year, Tolkien's publisher urged him to begin writing a sequel, and after several false starts, the story of the One Ring finally came to the author's mind. Over several years, what had begun as a concept for a relatively simple and straightforward sequel began transforming into something far bigger and more complex, bringing together worldbuilding and lore ideas from the rejected early drafts of The Silmarillion. Enter The Lord of the Rings, which was published in three volumes between 1954 and 1955. To this day, it's still generally remembered as the greatest and most foundational work of fantasy literature of the 20th century.

It's far and away one of the best epic fantasy books of all time, and for many years, it completely redefined and dominated the genre. Going forward and well into the '90s, almost all high fantasy books published were in some way either inspired by or directly trying to imitate Tolkien. However, though it's undoubtedly one of the greatest works of speculative fiction in history, there are four particular books which arguably do epic fantasy even better. Sprawling worlds on a grand scale, large ensemble casts, deep lore that readers can't get enough of, and sky-high stakes are all characteristics of these undeniable masterpieces, which certainly give Lord of the Rings a run for its money. In the end, literary appreciation is entirely subjective, but there's a very strong argument to be made that these gems all understood epic fantasy even better than Tolkien.

Canadian authors Steven Erikson and Ian Cameron Esslemont originally came up with the world of Malazan as a backdrop for role-playing games they made using a modified version of Advanced Dungeons & Dragons back in 1982. The world and its lore eventually grew so large that the duo wrote a movie script titled Gardens of the Moon, but after that failed to find interest, Erikson and Esslemont agreed to each write a series set in Malazan. Erikson wrote the Gardens of the Moon novel, which was published in 1999 and thus kicked off the now-legendary Malazan Book of the Fallen, one of the greatest high fantasy book series of all time. Erikson agreed to a contract for nine sequels as soon as he sold Gardens of the Moon, and the result is a gargantuan fantasy epic composed of over 3.3 million words.

Indeed, the Malazan series was so large and so pop-culturally significant that once its final volume came out, it felt like one of those fantasy books that marked the end of an era. We are, of course, talking about The Crippled God, one of the greatest fantasy epics of the 2010s. Erikson, writing as an educated and trained archaeologist and anthropologist, took the genre blueprint built by Tolkien decades prior and crafted a conclusive chapter that's as exhilarating as they come. Larger in scope, more structurally complex, and more thematically mature than The Lord of the Rings, The Crippled God masterfully brings together dozens of storylines and hundreds of characters into a single chaotic collision. The resulting novel is as morally complex as it is philosophically profound, and that's why it's a must-read for any fan of the epic fantasy genre.

The legendary Brandon Sanderson wrote throughout his undergraduate and graduate studies, with 12 novels already written by 2003 despite having no publisher or any offers of publication. It was in 2005 that Elantris, his debut novel, was finally published. Since then, Sanderson has become one of the most prolific speculative fiction writers of contemporary times, delivering several of the highest-rated books on Goodreads since 2000. Many of these books belong to his iconic Cosmere universe, composed of subseries as masterful as The Stormlight Archive. As exceptional as the series' first installment, The Way of Kings, was, it's the sequel that remains Sanderson's highest-rated book on Goodreads. It's Words of Radiance, the peak of 21st-century heroic high fantasy.

It doesn't feel quite as mythological as The Lord of the Rings, instead delivering a far more cinematic and character-driven experience that should appeal to anyone who tends to enjoy modern fantasy literature. For one, it's structurally perfect, a 1,000-page doorstop of a novel that nevertheless doesn't ever feel like it meanders. There's no fluff on the way to the Sanderlanche, a term fans have coined to describe the way Sanderson novels like Words of Radiance tend to culminate in fast-paced third acts where everything comes together in spectacular fashion to deliver a myriad of cathartic payoffs. Add to that a fascinating magic system, some of the most thematically layered and psychologically profound character writing that the genre has ever seen, and worldbuilding that even the most demanding epic fantasy readers should find satisfying, and you get a modern classic unlike any other. If there's any one fantasy novel that deserves to be called the best of the 21st century, it's this one.

Will George R. R. Martin ever finally finish writing A Song of Ice and Fire? Only time will tell. But even if the long-awaited The Winds of Winter never came, one thing would still remain undeniably true: A Storm of Swords is the last fantasy epic masterpiece of the 20th century. Back in the '90s, Martin had been wanting to take a stab at epic fantasy writing since reading the works of Tolkien, eventually coming up with the idea for A Song of Ice and Fire, now widely regarded as one of the greatest and most influential fantasy book series of modern times. It helped prove that the genre was more than ready to tell stories far darker, more mature, and more morally complex than what Tolkienesque high fantasy had been delivering for decades. The third book in the series is A Storm of Swords, still remembered by many as not only the best chapter in A Song of Ice and Fire so far, but also as one of the best fantasy novels ever written.

It is, at the very least, one of the best fantasy books since 2000; a bleak, exciting, brilliantly paced masterpiece that went on to win the 2001 Locus Award, be nominated for the Nebula Award for Best Novel, and become the first novel in the series to be nominated for the Hugo Award. There's no denying that there could never have been any Song of Ice and Fire—nor, by proxy, Storm of Swords—without Tolkien's influence in Martin's writing, but that's exactly what makes this novel so exceptional. Crafted in many ways as a direct subversion of many a Tolkienesque epic fantasy trope, A Storm of Swords is as politically complex as it is emotionally devastating. Balancing death, tragedy, action, and psychological realism to utter perfection, Martin delivered one of the most brilliant works of dark fantasy in history, culminating in an entire second half that's as breathtaking and propulsive as The Lord of the Rings' best battles.

It's complicated to compare ancient tales and myths to modern fantasy, since both genres are so dramatically different yet so essentially intertwined. Nonetheless, no one would call anybody crazy for saying that Homer's Odyssey does epic fantasy better than not only The Lord of the Rings, but practically any other epic fantasy book ever written. It is, after all, the fantasy epic par excellence, the poem that laid down the foundational blueprint for how Western writing would approach the fantasy and adventure genres forevermore. It established the core tropes of the genre long before "fantasy" actually existed as a properly distinct literary category, and is still a must-read for pretty much anybody and everybody with the ability to read a book.

Born as an oral tradition and not put into writing until around the mid-6th century BC, The Odyssey is the literal bedrock on which the entire Western epic literary tradition is built, which almost makes it unfair to compare any other subsequent masterpiece to it. Indeed, there aren't very many fantasy epics better than The Lord of the Rings, but if there's one whose superiority is pretty much undisputed, it's Homer's masterpiece. That's because, far from only being historically important, The Odyssey is so timeless that it's arguably still just as entertaining as any other epic fantasy masterwork. Intelligent, full of high-stakes set pieces, and infinitely analyzable from start to finish, it's the most perfect work of epic fantasy the world has ever seen.

The latest game in the Mafia series takes you back to 1900s Sicily, the birthplace of organized crime. You play Enzo, a fresh recruit in the Torrisi crime family, and must work your way up the ranks to become a "made man." Again, a lot of game for under 20 bucks.

Resident Evil Requiem combines elements from prior instalments to deliver one of the strongest franchise entries thus far. Its thrilling gameplay and stunning graphics keep you engaged from beginning to end.

Pragmata is a breath of fresh air thanks to its tactical combat, clever puzzles, and earnest sci-fi story. It proves that there's still innovation in the AAA space and is yet another winner from Capcom. And better yet, it's $20 off.

Star Wars Zero Company is a new turn-based tactics game where you recruit and lead a squad of operators and experience an original Star Wars story set during the Clone Wars. Lego Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight takes everything folks know about Batman from popular culture and filters it through the tried-and-true Lego formula. Whether you're a fan of Batman or Lego games, there's a lot to love in this charming adventure.

Control Resonant surpasses its excellent predecessor with a larger scope, both narratively and in gameplay. The melee-based combat is appropriately brutal and engaging, while the various skill trees offer deep customization. Aside from some confusing maps, this is an almost perfect action-based title.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a dark, brilliantly written vampire RPG with a superb prologue, a memorable cast, and inventive powers. Repetitive combat, a rough performance, and an insipid lead drag it down at times. A flawed, fascinating debut with cult classic written all over it — one that needs some post-launch patches, but kept us hooked regardless.

Step into the cockpit, take flight, and prepare for battle in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, the latest installment in the popular aerial combat franchise. Boasting a full single-player campaign and the series largest suite of online modes to date, not to mention stunning visuals and sound, it's the complete Ace Combat package.

007 First Light is the finest James Bond video game in nearly 30 years. Its cinematic single-player campaign is remarkable, delivering a gripping, quintessentially Bond story paired with some of the best action-adventure set pieces we’ve ever experienced. Whether you’re a longtime Bond fan or a newcomer, 007 First Light is unmissable.

Crimson Desert is one of the most ambitious single-player open-world games ever. It throws a ton of deep systems at you with almost no hand-holding, but once it clicks, the combat feels fantastic, and exploration feels rewarding. There’s enough content here to keep you busy for months on end. The story is pretty average, and the beginning can be brutal, but if you love big sandbox adventures, this one is worth the ride (and $69).

#3420. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3418. Two billion credentials publicly exposed, including everything needed for identity theft

A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” …

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler says that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

The “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler says, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

There’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting company to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

The best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

If you’re anything like me, you know the exact spiral that hits when your to-do list gets overwhelming. Your brain panics, you bounce between six smaller distractions to feel “productive,” and by 5 PM, you’ve somehow been busy all day while finishing absolutely nothing.

That’s why I was equal parts skeptical and desperate when I slipped on the Neurable One — a pair of over-ear ANC headphones that pack 12 EEG sensors directly into the ear cushions to read your brainwave patterns in real time.

Normally $499, Neurable has knocked $50 off for Black Friday, dropping them to $449 through November 30 — and crucially, there’s no subscription paywall locked behind the app. After testing them myself, I can confirm they genuinely work.

Save $50 on these brain-sensing ANC headphones that pack 12 dry EEG sensors into great-sounding 40mm beryllium drivers to track your focus, flag burnout before it hits, and keep you on task — with zero monthly subscription fees.

First, let’s clear up the sci-fi paranoia: these aren’t reading your thoughts. The fabric sensors knitted into the memory foam pads pick up electrical patterns from your brain (no messy gel or electrodes required) and translate them into a live Focus Tracking feed and a Brain battery fuel gauge in the companion app.

For a serial procrastinator (hi), having a live scoreboard for your attention is a game-changer. Starting a focus session turns staying on task into a literal workout for your brain: you can see the exact moment your concentration starts to drift, and the app nudges you to take Smart Brain Breaks before you hit the wall and doomscroll for an hour.

Since I started working with these on, I’m noticeably getting more done in my day without feeling fried by the evening. But the weirdest, most welcome side effect? My sleep score actually improved too — likely because I’m finally respecting my mental bandwidth during work hours instead of trying to brute force through exhaustion.

Normally, some party trick comes at the cost of forgetting to make a good pair of headphones. Fortunately, Neurable’s first all-in-house design gets the audio fundamentals right.

The custom 40mm beryllium drivers sound crisp, balanced and genuinely enjoyable for long workdays — tuned for clean, fatigue-free listening rather than bloated showroom bass.

Yes, the companion app’s EQ options are limited, which is going to bug the hardcore audio tweakers out there. But to my trained ears, the out-the-box audio quality is strong enough that it’s nowhere near a dealbreaker.

You also get solid active noise cancellation, a clear latency-free ambient mode and Bluetooth multipoint for hopping between your laptop and phone.

Before you do buy, I’d be doing a disservice in not pointing out a couple of downsides with these cans:

At $449, the Neurable one is still a serious investment — and if you just want the absolute lightest travel headphones with the greatest sound quality, there are plenty of mainstream options.

But if you struggle with distraction, burnout, or juggling ten half-finished tasks at once, these are the rare wellness wearable that actually earns its keep.

Getting a great sounding pair of ANC headphones and a personal focus coach for $50 off — with zero monthly fees — makes this one of the most interesting pair of cans I’ve tested this year, and my personal favorite Black Friday deal.

#3416. TIME’s Top 100 Photos of 2026 list includes a shot taken on iPhone 18 Pro

In September, Apple held a photography exhibition in New York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

The essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

Chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition)

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

“The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in New York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

The exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

You can view the full list of this year’s TIME 100 Photos right here.

#3415. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

#3413. CAD images suggest iPhone 18e will have an odd new camera design

CAD images of the iPhone 18e, said to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd new design for the camera bump.

If accurate, it would represent a big change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau …

The iPhone 17e was launched in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same.

The current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.

The site doesn’t share the images, but says that the camera bump looks similar to that of the M5 iPad Pro, shown below.

It’s unclear what might have prompted the change of design, especially as the site’s Filipe Espósito says he’s also seen CAD models for the standard model iPhone 18 or the iPhone Air 2, neither of which adopt it.

Previous reports have suggested that the only spec change with the iPhone 18e over its predecessor will be performance improvements thanks to the A20 chip.

#3411. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

#3409. iPhone Handoff: Here’s the latest on carrier availability and pricing

iPhone Handoff is a new feature in iOS 27 that lets you use the same phone number across two different iPhones. However, the feature requires carrier support, so it isn’t available to everyone. Here are the carriers that currently support iPhone Handoff and those that have promised support.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

With iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones. Your number automatically moves between the two phones, depending on which one you pick up. This includes calls, voicemail, messages, and Find My location.

Simply unlock whichever device you want to use and you’re ready to go. Other data synced with iCloud will automatically update across your devices. Third-party apps work across both devices, following each app’s own syncing behavior.

iPhone Handoff is available on iOS 27 and later. The phones must be connected to Wi-Fi, share the same Apple Account, use Messages in iCloud, and be signed into FaceTime and iMessage with the same Apple Account.

The biggest limiting factor of iPhone Handoff is that it requires carrier support. Currently, just three carriers support the feature:

What about carriers that are working on the feature? In the United States, Verizon has promised it “will support iPhone Handoff,” but it’s unclear when the feature will launch. Verizon says it will charge $10 per month for the service.

AT&T, meanwhile, has no plans to support iPhone Handoff. In a statement in September, the carrier said that its focus “remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” The carrier noted that there “could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” but that customers should use “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” instead.

No other carriers have promised support for iPhone Handoff, so it’s unclear how quickly the feature will expand around the world.

In my testing, iPhone Handoff works really well. I have it set up between my iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. I use the iPhone Duo 90% of the time, but when I do pick up my iPhone 18 Pro, my number instantly switches to it. There’s a cute animation that expands from the Dynamic Island, confirming that the number has moved.

Have you tried iPhone Handoff? Are you willing to pay extra for it? Let us know down in the comments.

#3407. Muse safety debate continues as the AI agent rolls out in the UK

The debate over the wisdom and safety of using Meta’s Muse AI agent continues as the app rolls out in the UK. It follows a warning by a number of regulatory bodies about the potential risks of AI agents …

Meta yesterday announced the UK availability of Muse.

Muse, Meta’s personal Al agent, is now available to adults in the UK. Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar. To get those jobs done you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.

A forum representing four different UK regulatory bodies last month issued a warning about the potential dangers involved in using AI agents. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum said:

AI agents may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce new ones. These risks may increase as the capabilities of personal agents grow and adoption rises. Questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection – for example the risk of fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information provided – must be addressed to ensure innovation develops in ways that earn and maintain public trust.

Meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse has accessed personal data without permission, insisting that users are in control and must approve important actions. The company has admitted to some “isolated incidents,” but says other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app while undergoing testing. In a new blog post, Meta says:

Muse only works with the apps and services you choose to connect it to, and you control the access it gets […] Once you’ve decided what Muse is connected to and what you want it to do, with your oversight, it can handle tasks like searching, comparing and planning for you. But before it does anything like sending an email or buying something, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your go-ahead. A separate security agent checks Muse’s actions and the information it sends out against the permissions you’ve granted. You can also choose how often it checks in with you in Settings.

At the time of writing, Muse remains the second most popular free app in Apple’s US App Store, with more than 10 million downloads. We reported yesterday that some banks are already blocking AI agents, while others are warning that they will not be responsible for the consequences of any actions taken by them.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.
